addressed_problems.content: The iterative magnitude pruning method employed to find winning-ticket subnetworks failed to produce subnetworks with single-model accuracy comparable to the dense baseline on tasks such as CoLA, QNLI, SST-2, and MNLI. As a result, the multi-ticket ensemble could not outperform the dense ensemble on those tasks. Therefore, more sophisticated or task-adaptive pruning algorithms and hyperparameter tuning are needed to reliably identify winning-ticket subnetworks that maintain high individual accuracy across a wider set of downstream tasks, thereby maximizing the potential of the multi-ticket ensemble.

The regularizers and mask-generation policies explored in this work (L1 regularizer with active masking and random masking) were simple heuristics. Although they improved structural and predictive diversity compared to naïve iterative magnitude pruning, they sometimes degraded single-model accuracy, and their design remains ad hoc. A key open challenge is to develop principled, parallelizable diversification methods that reliably maximize diversity among subnetworks without sacrificing the accuracy of individual members, going beyond the simple random and active masks tested here.

A satisfactory, general-purpose diversity metric that can predict ensemble performance is still lacking. The paper evaluated five popular diversity measures (Q statistic, ratio errors, negative double fault, disagreement measure, and correlation coefficient) but found that they only partially explain trends and do not fully account for ensemble gains. Finding a convenient and reliable diversity metric that directly relates to ensemble accuracy remains an open problem in the research community.

The paper's experiments used only a single pretrained BERT model. Prior work has shown that ensembles of models independently pretrained from scratch often outperform ensembles from a single pretrained model, but such comparisons require large computational resources to pretrain multiple models. Broader and more rigorous comparisons that use multiple independently pretrained models (e.g., from different seeds or configurations) would help contextualize the effectiveness of multi-ticket ensembles versus traditional ensembles of independently pretrained models; such large-scale investigations are left for future work.

Practical trade-offs and guidelines for selecting key hyperparameters—such as the pruning ratio, the coefficient of the L1 regularizer (τ), and other finetuning hyperparameters—across different tasks remain to be systematically characterized. In this work, the L1 coefficient was tuned on MRPC and then applied to other tasks without task-specific adjustment, which may limit performance on tasks where winning-ticket subnetworks are harder to find. A systematic study of hyperparameter sensitivity and task-specific tuning strategies is needed to make multi-ticket ensemble more robust and widely applicable.

Active masking, one of the regularizer policies explored, introduces a sequential dependence: the mask for each ensemble member depends on the surviving parameters of previous members. This prevents parallel training of the ensemble members, increasing computational overhead. Designing diversification methods that both encourage structural and predictive diversity and allow efficient parallel member training remains an open engineering and research question, particularly for scaling to larger ensembles and models.

The work addresses the practical and scientific problem of forming effective ensembles when only a single large-scale pretrained model is available. In modern NLP the pretrain-then-finetune paradigm produces high-performing models (e.g., BERT), but the computational cost of independently pretraining multiple models is prohibitive for most researchers and practitioners; consequently, ensembles are typically constructed by finetuning multiple copies of the same pretrained model. Prior approaches to produce diversity among such finetuned models—random initialization of task-specific heads, shuffling/SGD noise, or dropout—empirically yield only marginal parameter and prediction differences because finetuning often leaves parameters near their pretrained initialization. As a result, naïve ensembling of multiple finetuned models from the same pretrained initialization often gives limited gains compared to ensembles of independently pretrained models. Existing remedies such as adding large parameter noise can introduce diversity but at the cost of degraded individual-model accuracy. Separately, the lottery ticket literature indicates that dense networks can contain sparse “winning-ticket” subnetworks that can be finetuned to comparable accuracy, but it remained unclear whether distinct subnetworks extracted from the same pretrained model could (a) be found reliably for downstream finetuning, (b) be sufficiently diverse in structure and predictions to improve ensemble performance, and (c) be produced in a way that preserves single-model accuracy so ensemble gains are not canceled by lower member performance. These gaps—(i) lack of a method to obtain diverse yet accurate ensemble members from a single pretrained model, and (ii) lack of empirical evidence that different sparse subnetworks from one pretrained model yield larger ensemble gains than standard dense-model ensembles—motivate the present study.

nodes.content: In the setting where only a single pretrained model is available, researchers need an operational method that (a) produces multiple ensemble members that are both accurate after finetuning and distinct enough to yield ensemble gains, and (b) provides concrete training procedures amenable to implementation and evaluation. Prior to this work, iterative magnitude pruning and lottery-ticket findings suggested the existence of accurate subnetworks, but they did not provide a complete procedure for producing multiple distinct winning tickets from one pretrained model nor for steering pruning to increase inter-member diversity without harming accuracy. Moreover, a practical method must specify pruning schedules, the criterion for selecting parameters to prune, and mechanisms to encourage diverse surviving-parameter patterns across seeds without destroying the finetuning accuracy. The absence of such a concrete, reproducible workflow prevented controlled empirical study of whether subnetworks can enable effective ensembles from one pretrained model.

Iterative procedures that make each ensemble member dependent on earlier ones (e.g., active masking) introduce a sequential dependency that prevents parallel training and can complicate large-scale use. A seed-independent procedure that still produces diverse subnetworks is therefore needed. Prior to this work it was not demonstrated whether a simple, parallelizable random-masking policy could achieve ensemble gains comparable to or better than a sequential active masking policy while maintaining single-model accuracy.

The central empirical question is whether subnetworks extracted from a single pretrained model can produce ensembles that exceed the performance of ensembles built from dense finetunes of the same pretrained initialization. Before this study, ensembles finetuned from the same pretrained parameters were known to provide only marginal gains, leaving open whether a practical subnetwork-based approach could produce consistent, statistically significant improvements on standard benchmarks. Quantified experimental evidence with exact average single-model and ensemble accuracies is necessary to establish whether multi-ticket ensembles can realize this potential in practice.

For a practical ensemble method it is crucial to distinguish whether ensemble gains stem from stronger individual members or from complementary errors among members. If subnetworks only improved single-model accuracy, the ensemble advantage would be less informative about diversity. Prior to this analysis it was unclear whether using subnetworks would (a) degrade single-model performance and thus nullify ensemble gains, (b) improve single-model accuracy, or (c) preserve single-model accuracy but increase ensemble gains via higher inter-member diversity. Demonstrating which of these occurs requires a breakdown of single and ensemble accuracies.

Theoretical arguments posit that ensemble performance improves when members make complementary errors, but empirical validation requires measuring prediction diversity under multiple metrics because no single diversity score fully explains ensemble gains. Before this study it was not established whether subnetworks obtained from one pretrained model would produce measurably more diverse predictions than dense finetunes from the same initialization; such evidence is required to link subnetwork extraction to ensemble improvement.

Diversity in ensemble members can originate from structural differences in which parameters survive pruning. If iterative magnitude pruning with different seeds repeatedly selects nearly the same parameters, then ensemble diversity originating from structure will be limited. Prior to this work it was unclear whether standard iterative magnitude pruning would yield distinct masks across seeds or whether additional measures (regularizers or mask-design policies) would be required to produce structurally distinct subnetworks. Quantifying mask overlap clarifies whether methods actually produce diverse subnetwork architectures.

For multi-ticket ensemble to be broadly useful across tasks, pruning must produce subnetworks that preserve single-model accuracy; otherwise ensemble averaging cannot recover the baseline performance or exceed it. The current state before this work lacked a clear empirical account showing on which tasks naïve pruning finds adequate winning tickets and on which it does not, and lacked guidance about the necessity of more advanced pruning or tuning to make multi-ticket ensembles generally effective.

Reproducible empirical evaluation requires correct hyperparameter schedules; a mis-implemented learning-rate decay in prior code could have biased previous findings about pruning and finetuning behavior. Clarifying and correcting this implementation detail was necessary to ensure the reported experimental comparisons and conclusions are based on a standard linear-decay finetuning schedule that reaches zero.

Multi-Ticket Ensemble constructs an ensemble from a single pretrained model by (1) identifying and finetuning multiple sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) of the pretrained model and (2) averaging their outputs to form the ensemble output. The method operationalizes this idea using iterative magnitude pruning to find winning-ticket masks and two seed-dependent L1-regularization schemes to diversify pruning masks. In iterative magnitude pruning, a (sub)network is repeatedly finetuned, the 10% of parameters with lowest magnitudes are pruned at each pruning rehearsal, surviving parameters are reset to their original pretrained initialization, and the process is repeated until a target pruning ratio (e.g., 30%) is reached. The L1 regularizer for pruning adds the term τ||θ_s ⊙ l_s||_1 to the task loss during finetuning for pruning, where τ>0 is a scalar coefficient, ⊙ is element-wise product, θ_s denotes the parameters for seed s, and l_s ∈ R≥0^|θ| are element-wise coefficients that vary by seed. Two index policies for l_s are defined: (a) active masking, where for seed s_i, l_{s_i} = 1/(i-1) Σ_{j<i} m_{s_j} with m_{s_j} ∈ {0,1}^|θ| the surviving-parameter mask from seed s_j; (b) random masking, where for seed s_i, l_{s_i} = m_{s_i}^{rand} ∈ {0,1}^|θ| sampled element-wise from a Bernoulli distribution so that the probability of 0 equals the target pruning ratio. In the experiments, embeddings were not pruned and the L1 coefficient τ was decayed with the same scheduler as the learning rate.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 1 is a procedural description of the Multi-Ticket Ensemble method. The method is clearly operationalized with specific pruning ratios, regularizer forms, and masking policies. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the conclusion reports the method's existence rather than making a universal efficacy claim. The learning-rate scheduler correction (H1) ensures the finetuning procedure matches standard practice, strengthening the methodological soundness. The empirical success on MRPC and STS-B and the acknowledged limitations on other tasks are treated separately in other conclusions.

nodes.title: Multi-Ticket Ensemble method using iterative magnitude pruning and two L1-regularization policies (active and random masking)

nodes.content: Random masking, defined by using independently sampled binary masks m_{s_i}^{rand} as the L1 coefficient mask for each seed (i.e., l_s = m_{s_i}^{rand} with Bernoulli sampling at the target pruning ratio), enables independent, parallelizable training of ensemble members because each seed's regularization pattern is independent of other seeds. Empirically, on the BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) finetuning experiments on the MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus) and STS-B (Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark) tasks from GLUE, the random-masking variant RANDOM-LT (random-masking lottery-ticket ensemble) produced a larger average ensemble improvement (difference between ensemble accuracy and average single-model accuracy) than the sequential active-masking variant ACTIVE-LT (active-masking lottery-ticket ensemble), despite ACTIVE-LT explicitly discouraging reuse of previously surviving parameters.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2 has two components: parallelizability (a design property) and empirical effectiveness. The parallelizability claim is robust and directly follows from the independence of the random masks. However, the empirical effectiveness comparison is weakly supported due to a small and mixed average difference (P1) without a direct statistical test. No highlight directly mitigates this gap: H1 and H2 apply to both methods equally and do not distinguish them. The conclusion is therefore vulnerable on its comparative aspect: the evidence supports comparable effectiveness, not superiority.

nodes.title: Random masking enables parallelizable training and is empirically more effective than active masking on BERT MRPC and STS-B

nodes.content: On the GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation) benchmark tasks MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus) and STS-B (Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark) using the bert-base-uncased BERT model, ensembles of lottery-ticket subnetworks (BASE-LT: naïve iterative magnitude pruning; ACTIVE-LT: with active masking; RANDOM-LT: with random masking) outperform the standard dense-model baseline ensemble (BASELINE) and a bagging baseline (BAGGING, which trains dense models on different 90% training subsets) in ensemble improvement (difference between ensemble accuracy and average single-model accuracy) and in ensemble accuracy for some cases. The reported results, averaged over twenty finetuning seeds split into two groups of ten with exhaustive five-member ensemble combinations evaluated per group and then averaged, are as follows. MRPC single/ensemble/diff scores: BASELINE 83.48/84.34/+0.86; BAGGING 82.87/84.19/+1.32; BASE-LT 83.84/84.98/+1.14; ACTIVE-LT 83.22/84.60/+1.38; RANDOM-LT 83.53/85.05/+1.52. STS-B: BASELINE 88.35/89.04/+0.69; BAGGING 88.17/88.84/+0.68; BASE-LT 88.37/89.16/+0.79; ACTIVE-LT 88.39/89.32/+0.94; RANDOM-LT 88.49/89.35/+0.86. The improvements of the lottery-ticket methods (BASE-LT, ACTIVE-LT, RANDOM-LT) over BASELINE and BAGGING are statistically significant (p<0.001) in these cases.

metadata.narrative: The numerical results for conclusion 3 are grounded in a robust evaluation protocol (H2) that reduces estimation variance, and the learning-rate scheduler correction (H1) protects against artifacts from an incorrect schedule. These highlights support the credibility of the observed mean improvements (e.g., RANDOM-LT ensemble 85.05 vs BASELINE 84.34 on MRPC). However, the statistical significance claim is undermined by violations of independence and lack of multiple-testing correction (P2), meaning the confidence that the differences are not due to chance is overstated. The prior probability of 0.80 reflects the combination of reliable point estimates with uncertain significance.

nodes.title: Multi-ticket ensembles outperform dense ensembles on MRPC and STS-B with quantified gains

nodes.content: On the BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) experiments with bert-base-uncased on MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus) and STS-B (Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark), the average single-model accuracies of the lottery-ticket subnetworks (BASE-LT, ACTIVE-LT, RANDOM-LT) are similar to or not substantially better than the dense baseline (BASELINE) single-model accuracy, while the ensemble accuracies are higher; therefore the additional ensemble performance (difference between ensemble and single accuracy) is attributable to ensembling diversity rather than to improvements in individual member accuracy.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 4 is a direct readout of Table 1: single-model accuracies are similar across methods while ensemble diffs are larger for *-LT. This deduction does not rest on uncertain bridges beyond those already affecting the numbers themselves, which are supported by H1 (schedule correctness) and H2 (robust estimation). The conclusion's attribution of gains to diversity rather than improved single accuracy is a straightforward interpretation of the diff column and is well-supported by the data.

nodes.title: Ensemble gains arise from ensembling diverse subnetworks rather than improved single-model accuracy

nodes.content: On the MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus) task using bert-base-uncased BERT, ensembles composed of winning-ticket subnetworks (sparse subnetworks of the pretrained model that, after iterative magnitude pruning and finetuning, achieve accuracy comparable to the dense model) show larger prediction diversity according to five classification diversity metrics: Q statistic (Q), ratio errors (R), negative double fault (ND), disagreement measure (D), and correlation coefficient (C). Reported average values over five-member ensembles: BASELINE (dense model ensemble) Q=0.96, R=0.72, ND=-0.12, D=0.09, C=0.69; BASE-LT (lottery-ticket with naïve pruning) Q=0.93, R=1.00, ND=-0.11, D=0.10, C=0.62; ACTIVE-LT (lottery-ticket with active masking) Q=0.94, R=0.94, ND=-0.11, D=0.11, C=0.62; RANDOM-LT (lottery-ticket with random masking) Q=0.94, R=0.94, ND=-0.11, D=0.10, C=0.63. These metric values indicate that lottery-ticket subnetworks yield changes consistent with increased prediction diversity relative to the dense baseline.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 5 is supported by multi-metric evidence (H3) from five established diversity metrics, all showing consistent directional change toward increased diversity for *-LT on MRPC. This multi-metric consistency preempts concerns about metric-specific artifacts. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the claim is directly about the observed metric values, not about a causal explanation of ensemble gains. The prior probability is high, reflecting the strength of the convergent evidence.

nodes.title: Winning-ticket subnetworks produce more diverse predictions by multiple classification-diversity metrics

nodes.content: The structural diversity of subnetworks within a pretrained BERT model on MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus), measured by the pruning-mask intersection-over-union IoU = |m_i ∩ m_j| / |m_i ∪ m_j| between pairs of random seeds, varies by method: BASE-LT (lottery-ticket with naïve iterative magnitude pruning) produced pruning masks that were extremely similar across seeds (approximately 99% overlap), whereas ACTIVE-LT (lottery-ticket with active masking) and RANDOM-LT (lottery-ticket with random masking) produced substantially lower IoU values, indicating more diverse surviving-parameter patterns across seeds.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 6 reports direct structural measurements (IoU heatmap, H4) that show BASE-LT masks overlap at ~99% while regularizer methods produce lower overlap. This is a direct observational claim that is visually and quantitatively clear. No load-bearing weak points were identified. The conclusion is strongly supported by the presented measurement.

nodes.title: Subnetwork structural diversity measured by pruning-mask overlap (IoU) differs across methods; naive iterative pruning can produce highly overlapping masks

nodes.content: The benefit of multi-ticket ensemble depends on finding winning-ticket subnetworks (sparse subnetworks of the pretrained BERT model that achieve accuracy comparable to the dense model after iterative magnitude pruning and finetuning) that are sufficiently comparable in accuracy to the dense baseline. On several GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation) benchmark tasks (CoLA [Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability], QNLI [Question Natural Language Inference], SST-2 [Stanford Sentiment Treebank], MNLI [Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference]), the naïve iterative magnitude pruning often did not find subnetworks whose single-model accuracy matched the dense baseline (BASELINE), and consequently the final ensemble did not outperform the dense baseline ensemble on those tasks. More sophisticated pruning algorithms or task-specific tuning are needed to extend multi-ticket ensemble benefits to these tasks.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 7 is a self-acknowledged limitation supported by experimental results on CoLA, QNLI, SST-2, and MNLI where naive iterative magnitude pruning failed to find accurate winning tickets. The paper appropriately notes that more sophisticated pruning methods or tuning could address this, so the conclusion does not claim inherent impossibility. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the observation is directly reported and scoped to the tested configurations.

nodes.title: Limitation: ensemble fails when winning tickets are not comparably accurate; naive pruning is insufficient on many tasks

nodes.content: The implementation used for the multi-ticket ensemble experiments on BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) tasks corrected a bug in a prior public implementation (Chen et al., 2020): the linear learning-rate decay was fixed so that the learning rate reaches zero at the end of finetuning, matching common practice and the published description. This correction was applied before running the reported experiments.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 8 is a factual correction of a previously published learning rate scheduler implementation, with the corrected version used in the paper's experiments. The bug and its fix are described in Appendix B and directly verified. There is no uncertainty, and the conclusion is fully supported.

nodes.title: Implementation correction to prior work's learning-rate scheduler

nodes.content: On the GLUE tasks MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus) and STS-B (Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark) using bert-base-uncased BERT, with exhaustive five-member ensembles formed from twenty random seeds split into two groups of ten and averaged over groups, the ensemble improvement (difference between ensemble accuracy and average single-model accuracy) for RANDOM-LT (lottery-ticket with random masking) is 1.52 on MRPC and 0.86 on STS-B, while for ACTIVE-LT (lottery-ticket with active masking) it is 1.38 on MRPC and 0.94 on STS-B. The simple average across the two tasks is 1.19 for RANDOM-LT and 1.16 for ACTIVE-LT, and no direct statistical test comparing RANDOM-LT and ACTIVE-LT is reported.

metadata.failure_mode: If the claimed greater effectiveness of RANDOM-LT is not robust, then conclusion 2's assertion that RANDOM-LT is "empirically more effective" loses its justification. The surviving support is only that RANDOM-LT is parallelizable and achieves ensemble gains comparable to ACTIVE-LT (with mixed relative performance). The specific claim of superiority over active masking would be unsupported, reducing the conclusion to a statement about design properties (parallelizability) and a finding of comparable—not superior—performance.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper asserts that RANDOM-LT is "more effective" than ACTIVE-LT, but the evidence is weak: on one task (STS-B) ACTIVE-LT outperforms RANDOM-LT, on the other task the advantage is small, and the average difference (0.03 points) is negligible relative to the observed seed-level variation. Without a direct significance test (e.g., paired t-test across runs or correction for multiple comparisons across methods), the observed average advantage could easily arise from noise. The paper's own footnote (3) acknowledges that the independence assumption required for standard testing is violated, further undermining any implicit inferential claim.

nodes.title: No direct statistical test reported for RANDOM-LT versus ACTIVE-LT comparison on MRPC and STS-B

nodes.content: In the BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) experiments using bert-base-uncased on MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus) and STS-B (Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark), the lottery-ticket ensemble methods (BASE-LT: naïve iterative magnitude pruning; ACTIVE-LT: active masking; RANDOM-LT: random masking) are compared to the dense baseline ensemble (BASELINE) using Student's t-test with p<0.001 reported as significant. It is noted that not all evaluation samples satisfy the independence assumption for the t-test, and no correction for multiple comparisons across the three or four method variants (BASE-LT, ACTIVE-LT, RANDOM-LT, and sometimes BAGGING [bagging baseline]) and two datasets is applied.

metadata.failure_mode: If the reported statistical significance is not valid, conclusion 3's claim of "statistically significant (p<0.001)" outperformance is not substantiated. The numerical point estimates (e.g., RANDOM-LT ensemble 85.05 vs BASELINE 84.34 on MRPC) remain as observed values, but the paper cannot assert with high confidence that the improvements are not due to chance. The conclusion would be weakened from "significantly outperforms" to "tends to outperform based on observed mean differences."
metadata.weakness_reason: The t-test requires independent observations, but the evaluations share the same test set, use overlapping training data (random seeds from the same pretrained initialization), and the ensemble combinations are extensive and overlapping. The multiple comparisons across methods and datasets inflate the chance of false positives. The paper acknowledges the issue but does not apply robust corrections (e.g., Bonferroni, permutation test with blocked resampling). Therefore the reported p-values are likely smaller than the true significance level, overstating confidence in the outperformance.

nodes.title: T-test assumption of independent samples not fully satisfied and no multiple comparison correction applied

nodes.content: The implementation corrects a bug in the publicly available code of Chen et al. (2020) where the linear learning-rate decay did not reach zero at the end of finetuning, ensuring that in the reported experiments the learning rate decays linearly from 2e-5 to zero over 3 epochs, matching the standard finetuning practice and the description in the original lottery-ticket work.

metadata.credit: This correction preempts the failure mode where the observed pruning and finetuning behavior could be an artifact of an incorrect learning-rate schedule (e.g., still high learning rate at the end preventing proper convergence or affecting mask selection). By ensuring the finetuning schedule matches the intended common practice, it underwrites the reliability of all downstream results—single-model accuracies, mask identities, and ensemble gains—for conclusions 1 (method correctness) and 3 (empirical results). Without this fix, any of the experimental findings could have been confounded by the mismatched schedule, so the correction is load-bearing for the experimental credibility.

nodes.title: Learning rate scheduler correction

nodes.content: The experiment evaluates ensemble performance by training twenty random seeds, splitting them into two groups of ten, and exhaustively computing all possible ensemble combinations of size 2 to 5 (i.e., C(10,5)=252 combinations per group), then averaging the results across the two groups and across combinations, providing aggregated statistics with reduced estimation variance.

metadata.credit: This exhaustive evaluation protocol guards against the failure mode of reporting ensemble performance based on a single or small number of member combinations, which could have high variance and produce non-representative results. By averaging over all possible five-member ensembles from two independent groups, the reported ensemble accuracy (e.g., 85.05 for RANDOM-LT on MRPC) is a low-variance estimate of the expected performance of five-member ensembles from the method. This strengthens the quantitative grounding of conclusion 3's comparative claims, as the numbers are less likely to be artifacts of a favorable seed combination.

nodes.title: Exhaustive ensemble evaluation

nodes.content: On MRPC, five established classification diversity metrics—Q statistic (Yule, 1900), ratio errors (Aksela, 2003), negative double fault (Giacinto and Roli, 2001), disagreement measure (Skalak, 1996), and correlation coefficient (Kuncheva and Whitaker, 2003)—are computed for pairs of members in BASELINE and *-LT ensembles; all five metrics show directional changes consistent with increased prediction diversity for *-LT (Q decreases from 0.96 to 0.93–0.94, R increases from 0.72 to 0.94–1.00, ND increases from -0.12 to -0.11, D increases from 0.09 to 0.10–0.11, C decreases from 0.69 to 0.62–0.63).

metadata.credit: The use of multiple independently defined diversity metrics that all move in the same direction strengthens conclusion 5—that winning-ticket subnetworks produce more diverse predictions than dense networks. If only a single metric were used, the result could be metric-specific. The consistent pattern across five metrics preempts the failure mode where the observed diversity increase is an artifact of a particular metric's shortcomings. The paper's own caveat that existing diversity scores do not fully explain ensemble performance does not reduce this strength; the conclusion is about the existence of greater diversity, not about its causal role in ensemble gains.

nodes.title: Multi-metric diversity measurement

nodes.content: The overlap ratio of pruning masks (intersection over union, IoU) between pairs of seeds for BASE-LT on MRPC is approximately 99%, while ACTIVE-LT and RANDOM-LT yield substantially lower IoU values as shown in the heatmap of Figure 4.

metadata.credit: This direct structural quantification provides concrete evidence for the claim in conclusion 6 that BASE-LT produces highly overlapping masks whereas the regularizer-based methods increase structural diversity. Without this measurement, the claim would rely on indirect inference from prediction diversity. The IoU metric directly measures parameter-level overlap, giving independent support that the regularizers affect which parameters survive pruning. The 99% figure for BASE-LT is particularly striking and underlines the need for explicit diversification.

nodes.title: IoU mask overlap visualization

steps.reasoning: Define the ensemble output and model notation: let $f(x; \boldsymbol{\theta})$ be the output of a model with parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ given input $\boldsymbol{x}$, and let an ensemble of member parameter vectors $\mathcal{M}=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{|\mathcal{M}|}\}$ produce the averaged output $f_{\mathcal{M}}(\boldsymbol{x})=\sum_{\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathcal{M}} f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta})/|\mathcal{M}|$ (notation introduced in the paper's discussion of standard ensembling).

Introduce the Multi-Ticket Ensemble idea as a construction: construct an ensemble from a single pretrained model by (a) identifying multiple sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) of the single pretrained model, each corresponding to a mask and parameter subset, and finetuning these subnetworks separately; and (b) averaging their outputs $f(\cdot;\boldsymbol{\theta}_{s})$ across seeds $s$ to form the ensemble output $f_{\mathcal{M}}(\cdot)$. This framing is the central method proposal motivating the specific algorithmic choices that follow.

Define symbols used for pruning and regularization: let $\boldsymbol{\theta}_s$ denote the parameter vector (trainable parameters) when finetuning with random seed $s$, let $\boldsymbol{m}_{s}\in\{0,1\}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ denote the binary pruning mask indicating surviving parameters for seed $s$ (1 for surviving, 0 for pruned), let element-wise product be $\odot$, and let $\boldsymbol{l}_s\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ denote nonnegative element-wise coefficients used as per-seed weights for an $L_1$ regularizer; let $\tau>0$ be the scalar coefficient of the $L_1$ regularizer. These symbols are used in the paper where the authors introduce pruning and regularization.

Describe the iterative magnitude pruning procedure used to identify winning tickets: (a) start from the pretrained dense parameter initialization (the pretrained model used for finetuning); (b) perform finetuning of the network on the downstream task using a chosen random seed; (c) identify the 10% of parameters with the smallest magnitudes in the finetuned parameters and mark them as targets to prune for that rehearsal; (d) prune those parameters (i.e., form a subnetwork by zeroing or masking them), then reset the surviving parameters to their original pretrained initialization (the original values before finetuning); (e) repeat the finetune-prune-reset rehearsals until the cumulative pruning reaches the target pruning ratio; and (f) in the experiments the authors used a target pruning ratio of 30% and used 10% pruning at each rehearsal. This iterative procedure is the authors' operationalization of the lottery-ticket iterative magnitude pruning approach they cite.
Frankle and Carbin (2019)
Figure 2

State the reset-to-pretrained-initialization step explicitly as part of iterative magnitude pruning: after each pruning rehearsal the surviving parameters are reset to their originally-initialized values from the pretrained model (this reset differs from continuing training from post-finetuning weights and is explicit in the rehearsal description).
Figure 2

Specify the $L_1$-regularization scheme used during finetuning-for-pruning: during finetuning (the rehearsals used to search pruning masks) the authors add the regularization term $\tau\lVert \boldsymbol{\theta}_s \odot \boldsymbol{l}_s\rVert_1$ to the task loss, where $\tau$ is a positive scalar coefficient, $\odot$ denotes element-wise product, $\boldsymbol{\theta}_s$ are the finetuned parameters for seed $s$, and $\boldsymbol{l}_s$ is a nonnegative vector of element-wise coefficients that varies by seed and determines which parameters are encouraged to have small magnitude. This term is intended to softly penalize magnitudes of selected parameters and thus bias which parameters will be pruned in subsequent rehearsals.

Define the two index-policy variants for choosing the per-seed coefficient vector $\boldsymbol{l}_s$: (a) Active masking (sequential/affirmative policy): for the $i$-th seed $s_i$ use $\boldsymbol{l}_{s_i}=\frac{1}{i-1}\sum_{j<i}\boldsymbol{m}_{s_j}$, where $\boldsymbol{m}_{s_j}\in\{0,1\}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ is the surviving-parameter mask from previously processed seed $s_j$; this means parameters that survived earlier seeds receive stronger $L_1$ weight for later seeds, which discourages reuse of previously surviving parameters. (b) Random masking (parallelizable policy): for the $i$-th seed $s_i$ sample an independent random binary mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{s_i}^{\mathrm{rand}}\in\{0,1\}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ element-wise from a Bernoulli distribution with probability of 0 equal to the target pruning ratio, and set $\boldsymbol{l}_{s_i}=\boldsymbol{m}_{s_i}^{\mathrm{rand}}$; this makes the per-seed regularization pattern independent across seeds.

Clarify implementation details and exceptions used in experiments: the embedding layer was not pruned (the authors explicitly state they did not prune embeddings), the $L_1$ coefficient $\tau$ was decayed using the same scheduler as the learning rate during finetuning, and hyperparameters such as pruning ratio (30%), rehearsal pruning fraction (10% per rehearsal), and scheduler choices follow the experimental setting described in the implementation appendix and main experiment descriptions.
Table A (implementation settings in Appendix)

Summarize the operational Multi-Ticket Ensemble method as implemented in the experiments: use iterative magnitude pruning (as above) to find multiple winning-ticket masks across different random seeds, optionally use seed-dependent $L_1$ regularizers with either active masking or random masking to diversify pruning masks, finetune the resulting subnetworks from the original pretrained initialization, and average their outputs to form the ensemble. This operationalization is the concrete procedure the paper uses to evaluate Multi-Ticket Ensemble.

Treat the result of Conclusion 1 (the Multi-Ticket Ensemble method, the definition of random masking and active masking, and the operational procedures for pruning and regularization) as known and available for use in the derivation of this conclusion.

Explain why random masking enables independent, parallelizable training: random masking sets each seed's $L_1$ coefficient vector $\boldsymbol{l}_{s_i}$ to an independently sampled binary mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{s_i}^{\mathrm{rand}}$ that does not depend on any other seed's surviving-parameter masks; because $\boldsymbol{l}_{s_i}$ does not require information from previously computed masks, the finetuning and mask-search for each seed can be performed independently and in parallel, unlike active masking where $\boldsymbol{l}_{s_i}=\frac{1}{i-1}\sum_{j<i}\boldsymbol{m}_{s_j}$ depends sequentially on prior seeds.
Section 3.2 (Random Masking description)

Present the empirical evidence the authors use to compare RANDOM-LT and ACTIVE-LT: the authors report finetuning experiments with BERT on MRPC and STS-B, evaluating exhaustive five-member ensembles among twenty finetuning seeds and averaging results; Table 1 summarizes single-model accuracy ('single'), ensemble accuracy ('ens.'), and ensemble improvement ('diff.') for BASELINE, BAGGING, BASE-LT, ACTIVE-LT, and RANDOM-LT, while the text explicitly states that RANDOM-LT is "simpler but more effective" than ACTIVE-LT on average.
Table 1

Describe the specific numeric evidence from Table 1 that the authors cite in support of RANDOM-LT's empirical effectiveness on MRPC and STS-B: for MRPC the reported average 'diff.' values are BASELINE +0.86, BAGGING +1.32, BASE-LT +1.14, ACTIVE-LT +1.38, RANDOM-LT +1.52 (RANDOM-LT largest); for STS-B the reported 'diff.' values are BASELINE +0.69, BAGGING +0.68, BASE-LT +0.79, ACTIVE-LT +0.94, RANDOM-LT +0.86 (ACTIVE-LT largest for STS-B). The authors summarize these mixed per-task numbers by asserting that RANDOM-LT produced larger ensemble gains on average than ACTIVE-LT across their BERT finetuning experiments.
Table 1

Conclude two linked points drawing from the definition and the empirical evidence: (a) random masking enables independent, parallelizable training of ensemble members because each seed's regularization mask $\boldsymbol{l}_{s_i}=\boldsymbol{m}_{s_i}^{\mathrm{rand}}$ is independent of other seeds; and (b) empirically, according to the reported BERT finetuning experiments on MRPC and STS-B and the authors' textual summary, RANDOM-LT produced larger ensemble gains on average than ACTIVE-LT despite ACTIVE-LT's explicit discouragement of reusing previously surviving parameters.
(authors' textual summary in Section 4.1 and Section 3.2)

Treat as known the Multi-Ticket Ensemble method (Conclusion 1), the finding that winning-ticket subnetworks produce more diverse predictions by multiple metrics (Conclusion 5), and the limitation that benefits require comparably accurate winning tickets (Conclusion 7); these upstream conclusions are starting points for establishing the comparative performance claim on MRPC and STS-B.

Describe the experimental evaluation setup that produced the comparative results: the authors finetuned models following the transformers/BERT finetuning settings, used twenty different random seeds, evaluated exhaustive five-member ensembles formed from those seeds (i.e., exhaustive combinations of five members among prepared groups), averaged the results across the two groups of ten seeds and across all ensembles, and performed Student's t-test for statistical significance; the experiments compare four finetuning schemes (BASELINE, BASE-LT, ACTIVE-LT, RANDOM-LT) and a BAGGING baseline.
Table 1

Present the reported numeric results for BERT on MRPC (averaged over seeds and ensemble combinations) that the authors use to support the claim: BASELINE single/ens./diff = 83.48/84.34/+0.86; BAGGING 82.87/84.19/+1.32; BASE-LT 83.84/84.98/+1.14; ACTIVE-LT 83.22/84.60/+1.38; RANDOM-LT 83.53/85.05/+1.52. These numbers are taken directly from the reported Table 1 for MRPC.
Table 1

Present the reported numeric results for BERT on STS-B (averaged over seeds and ensemble combinations) that the authors use to support the claim: BASELINE single/ens./diff = 88.35/89.04/+0.69; BAGGING 88.17/88.84/+0.68; BASE-LT 88.37/89.16/+0.79; ACTIVE-LT 88.39/89.32/+0.94; RANDOM-LT 88.49/89.35/+0.86. These numbers are taken directly from the reported Table 1 for STS-B.
Table 1

State the statistical-significance claim the authors make about the *-LT methods' improvements: the authors report that the multi-ticket ensemble variants (*-LT) outperform BASELINE and BAGGING significantly with $p<0.001$ for the MRPC and STS-B cases reported, indicating that the observed ensemble improvements are statistically validated in their experimental analysis.
authors' Student's t-test statements in Section 4 and Table 1

Conclude that, based on the experimental setup, the reported numeric results, and the statistical tests, ensembles composed of lottery-ticket subnetworks (BASE-LT, ACTIVE-LT, RANDOM-LT) outperform the standard dense-model baseline ensemble (BASELINE) and the BAGGING baseline in ensemble improvement (the 'diff.' column), and in some cases the ensemble accuracy itself is higher; thus the authors substantiate their claim with the reported averages and significance tests on MRPC and STS-B for BERT.

Treat as known the empirical performance numbers in Table 1 and the experimental setup and statistical tests established in Conclusion 3; these upstream results are the starting point for attributing ensemble gains to diversity rather than single-model improvements.
Table 1

Compare the 'single' and 'ens.' columns in the reported results to assess whether ensemble gains arise from improved single-model accuracy or from ensembling: note that in Table 1 the 'single' accuracies for *-LT methods are similar to the BASELINE single accuracies (for MRPC: BASELINE single 83.48 vs BASE-LT 83.84, ACTIVE-LT 83.22, RANDOM-LT 83.53; for STS-B: BASELINE single 88.35 vs BASE-LT 88.37, ACTIVE-LT 88.39, RANDOM-LT 88.49), whereas the 'ens.' values are higher for *-LT methods than baseline.
Table 1

Use the authors' explicit textual statement to justify the attribution: the authors state that "the improvements of *-LT are attributable to ensembling (diff.) rather than to any performance gains of the individual models (single)" and also present Figure 3 showing that while single models of *-LT have accuracy similar to BASELINE, gains appear when ensembling them (Figure 3 plots relative gains as a function of the number of ensemble members).
Figure 3

Conclude that, because the single-model accuracies of the subnetworks remain similar to or not substantially better than the dense baseline while the ensemble accuracies increase, the additional performance of the *-LT ensembles is attributable to increased ensemble diversity among members (the 'diff.' column) rather than to systematic improvements in individual member accuracy.

Treat as known the Multi-Ticket Ensemble method and its mask/regularizer definitions from Conclusion 1 and the structural-diversity observations (IoU differences across methods) from Conclusion 6; these are the upstream results used to interpret prediction diversity.

Explain which prediction-diversity metrics the authors used and their directional interpretation: the authors evaluated five classification diversity metrics — Q statistic (Q), ratio errors (R), negative double fault (ND), disagreement measure (D), and correlation coefficient (C) — and indicated for each whether lower ($\downarrow$) or higher ($\uparrow$) values correspond to greater prediction diversity in their Table 2 (for example, Q and C are labeled with $\downarrow$ meaning lower values indicate more diversity, while R and D are $\uparrow$ meaning higher indicates more diversity).
Kuncheva and Whitaker (2003); Cruz et al. (2020) (as cited by the authors)

Present the empirical numeric values reported in Table 2 for MRPC for each method and metric: BASELINE: Q=0.96, R=0.72, ND=-0.12, D=0.09, C=0.69; BASE-LT: Q=0.93, R=1.00, ND=-0.11, D=0.10, C=0.62; ACTIVE-LT: Q=0.94, R=0.94, ND=-0.11, D=0.11, C=0.62; RANDOM-LT: Q=0.94, R=0.94, ND=-0.11, D=0.10, C=0.63. These figures are the authors' measured averages across relevant seeds and ensemble combinations for MRPC.
Table 2

Interpret the metric changes relative to the BASELINE according to the indicated directions: (a) Q decreased from 0.96 (BASELINE) to 0.93–0.94 for *-LT methods, which is consistent with increased diversity because Q is labeled $\downarrow$; (b) R increased from 0.72 (BASELINE) to 0.94–1.00 for *-LT methods, consistent with increased diversity because R is labeled $\uparrow$; (c) ND moved from -0.12 to -0.11 (less negative) for *-LT, which the authors indicate corresponds with the directional expectation for diversity (ND labeled $\downarrow$, so the small change is interpreted in context as consistent with increased diversity); (d) D increased from 0.09 to 0.10–0.11 for *-LT, consistent with increased diversity because D is labeled $\uparrow$; (e) C decreased from 0.69 to 0.62–0.63 for *-LT, consistent with increased diversity because C is labeled $\downarrow$. These directional comparisons are the basis for the authors' statement that *-LT subnetworks yield metric changes consistent with increased prediction diversity relative to the dense baseline.
Table 2

Connect structural diversity (from known Conclusion 6) with prediction diversity: given that ACTIVE-LT and RANDOM-LT showed lower pruning-mask IoU (more structural diversity) and that the *-LT methods show metric changes consistent with increased prediction diversity, conclude that winning-ticket subnetworks produce more diverse predictions by the reported classification-diversity metrics on MRPC.
Treat the procedural components of conclusion 1 (iterative magnitude pruning, masks $\boldsymbol{m}_{s}$) as known starting points for analyzing structural diversity measured by pruning-mask overlap.

Define the structural-diversity metric used by the authors: for two binary pruning masks $m_i$ and $m_j$, define the overlap ratio (intersection-over-union) $\mathrm{IoU}=\frac{|m_i\cap m_j|}{|m_i\cup m_j|}$, which measures the fraction of parameters that are simultaneously surviving in both masks relative to those surviving in at least one of them; this definition is the one used and cited by the authors.
Chen et al. (2020) (as cited by the authors)

Describe the empirical measurements the authors present for mask overlap: the authors computed pairwise IoU values for the five random seeds' pruning masks $\{\boldsymbol{m}_{s_1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{m}_{s_5}\}$ on MRPC and visualized them in a matrix (Figure 4), where lower (yellower) values indicate more dissimilar masks and higher values indicate more similar masks.
Figure 4

Report the specific empirical observations from that visualization and text: (a) BASE-LT (naïve iterative magnitude pruning without the seed-dependent regularizers) produced pruning masks that were extremely similar across seeds, reported as approximately 99% overlap (IoU ≈ 0.99) on MRPC; (b) ACTIVE-LT and RANDOM-LT, both using seed-dependent $L_1$ regularizers, produced substantially lower IoU values (visually shown as more yellow/lower overlap in the reported overlap matrix), indicating more diverse surviving-parameter patterns across seeds.
Figure 4

Conclude that naive iterative magnitude pruning can produce highly overlapping masks while the regularizer-based variants (active and random masking) produce more structural diversity in surviving-parameter patterns as measured by pairwise IoU, based on the reported ~99% IoU for BASE-LT and visually substantially lower IoU for ACTIVE-LT and RANDOM-LT in the authors' results.

Present the authors' central limitation statement as derived directly from their empirical findings: the benefit of multi-ticket ensemble depends on finding winning-ticket subnetworks that are sufficiently comparable in accuracy to the dense baseline; when winning tickets are less accurate, the ensemble benefit often fails because lower single-model accuracy can cancel ensembling gains.

Cite the specific empirical tasks where the naïve iterative magnitude pruning often failed to produce sufficiently accurate winning-ticket subnetworks: the authors list CoLA, QNLI, SST-2, and MNLI as tasks where naive iterative magnitude pruning did not find subnetworks whose single-model accuracy matched the dense baseline; as a result the final ensemble did not outperform the dense baseline ensemble on those tasks in the authors' experiments.

Report the authors' observed nuance about RANDOM-LT in such failure cases: even when the naive pruning failed to find accurate winning tickets, RANDOM-LT often yielded a higher ensembling improvement component ('diff.'), but the degradation in single-model accuracy caused the total ensemble accuracy not to surpass the dense baseline; BAGGING also failed to improve in these cases according to the authors' observations.

Record the authors' recommendation and stated need for future work: to extend multi-ticket ensemble benefits to tasks where naive pruning is insufficient, more sophisticated pruning algorithms (the authors cite related pruning literature) or task-specific tuning would be needed to find better winning-ticket subnetworks without sacrificing single-model performance.
Blalock et al. (2020); Sanh et al. (2020)

Note that the authors explicitly acknowledge prior reports of related findings by other studies and clarify that their observations are not contradicted by those reports: the authors include footnotes discussing prior definitions of "winning ticket" and remark that some prior studies found subnetworks slightly worse than dense networks, aligning with the authors' conclusion that naive pruning can be insufficient on many tasks.

State the implementation provenance and the discovered issue: the experiments' implementation was derived from Chen et al. (2020)'s public implementation (the authors cite that repository), and the authors found a bug in that implementation related to the learning-rate scheduler.
Chen et al. (2020)

Describe the precise bug and the expected behavior: the intended learning-rate schedule is linear decay from the initial value to zero by the end of finetuning (the common setting and the description in Chen et al.'s paper), but in Chen et al.'s public implementation the linear-decay learning rate did not reach zero at the end of finetuning and instead remained at a significant level.
Appendix B (learning-rate scheduler discussion)

Explain the authors' corrective action and its application: the authors corrected the implementation so that the learning-rate linear decay reaches zero at the end of finetuning (matching the published description and common practice), and they applied this corrected scheduler before running the reported experiments.
Appendix B (learning-rate scheduler discussion)

open_questions.content: The paper acknowledges multiple unresolved issues and directions for future work: (1) The need for more sophisticated or task-adaptive pruning algorithms and hyperparameter tuning to reliably find winning-ticket subnetworks whose single-model accuracy matches dense baselines across a wider set of tasks (the naïve iterative magnitude pruning used here failed on CoLA, QNLI, SST-2, MNLI in the reported experiments). (2) The design of regularizers and mask-generation policies that maximize structural and predictive diversity without degrading individual-model performance remains open; in particular, finding principled, parallelizable diversification methods beyond the simple random and active masks explored here is an unresolved challenge. (3) A satisfactory, general-purpose diversity metric that predicts ensemble performance is still lacking; existing metrics partially explain trends but do not fully account for ensemble gains. (4) Broader and more rigorous comparisons that use multiple independently pretrained models (which requires large computational resources) would help contextualize ensembles made from a single pretrained model versus ensembles of independently pretrained models; such large-scale investigations are left for future work. (5) Practical trade-offs and guidelines for selecting pruning ratios, $L_1$ coefficients, and other finetuning hyperparameters across tasks remain to be systematically characterized. Finally, (6) active masking's sequential dependence limits parallel training; designing diversification methods that both encourage diversity and allow efficient parallel member training remains an open engineering and research question.
